extracted.intended_audience: improvisers, improv teachers, and theatre students learning character work
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and exercises for creating, committing to, and developing characters in improvisational theatre, with rules-of-thumb for running workshops and avoiding common pitfalls (blocking, canceling, over-reliance on props/slips).

rubrics_metrics.name: Play strong attitudes and physicality
rubrics_metrics.description: Put the emphasis on playing strong attitudes; physical choices and attitudes make any setting interesting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: an obsessively tidy shopkeeper, a drunk Glaswegian customer; synthesizes attitude work (Characters From A Hat) and platform/space work (Go Through An Unusual Door). Strong attitudes give the other player clear offers to react to and raise audience interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin with a purpose (super-objective)
rubrics_metrics.description: Start characters with a clear purpose or 'super-objective' (what the character is almost always trying to achieve in life).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use lists of behaviors that express the super-objective (e.g., 'to be thought clever' → correct people, quote statistics, carry gadgets). This externalizes attitude and gives improvisers permission to act, but beware of over-reliance on the list as a crutch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use slips of paper as permission, not as a constant crutch
rubrics_metrics.description: Slips give 'permission' to adopt alien or inappropriate behavior and make character choices obvious, but must not occupy the improviser's entire focus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer slips kept private to encourage internalisation; consider 'training wheels' sessions where slips are revealed and discussed, then remove slips gradually. Tom's Characters From A Hat combines slips with in-scene flexibility to avoid constant checking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Play your own sex (adapt the slip to your gender)
rubrics_metrics.description: When given a character descriptor that implies the opposite sex, create the equivalent version for your own gender rather than playing ambiguous gender.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This avoids confusion—e.g., a male actor getting 'slutty secretary' should find the male version. This often produces strong, clear characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept endowments and make assumptions about partners
rubrics_metrics.description: The slip may define your job but your partner can endow you with additional facts; accept these endowments rather than blocking them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the slip says 'nervous new boy' but your partner endows you as the director, you are the director with the attitude of a nervous new boy. Don't use the slip to block offers from partners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be specific early—establish basic scene facts quickly
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish key information at the start so the audience can engage: Have these people met? What's the hierarchical relationship? Whose space is it?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coach should encourage specificity; good early specifics raise audience interest and make subsequent changes meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical and costume details should aid, not distract
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid ostentatious or distracting clothing/jewellery and dress simply so the audience can focus on character and eyes (e.g., use contact lenses if needed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obscene t-shirts, exposed breasts, or very distracting items divert audience attention and make it harder for them to buy into characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on nudity or identical dressing to solve casting/preconception issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Stripping or dressing the cast identically is not an effective solution to audience preconceptions; such tactics either distract or suppress individuality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audiences expect actors to play different roles in improv; encourage visible commitment to the role instead of provocative or uniform costuming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the environment/space (platform) to inspire character choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Build a believable environment with small props/arrangement (chairs, desk) so physical offers flow naturally and suggest character details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good space work answers 'what is this space like?' and helps actors discover objects or habits (e.g., dumbbells in a filing cabinet) that extend character choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid blocking and bargaining
rubrics_metrics.description: Blocking (rejecting offers) and bargaining (negotiating within the scene) gum up scenes and kill energy; they often arise from fear of delivering a simple brief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by shoe shop: actors who block by refusing offers ('I’m afraid not') or bargaining ('I’ll pay triple') create stagnant scenes. Coach should steer players away from these behaviours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliver the brief—don't fear simple endings
rubrics_metrics.description: Completing a simple transaction or brief (e.g., buy and sell a pair of shoes) is not failure; fear of brevity drives blocking and artificial complication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate quick, committed delivery of the brief without blocking and with entertaining character work—the scene can still be interesting even if the surface event is simple.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make promises to the audience through character choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical/attitudinal choices should make promises (predictable expectations) that the scene can then break or fulfil, creating dramatic/comedic payoffs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a perfectly orderly shop promises that someone will bring chaos; these promises narrow imaginative search and create clear trajectories for the other player.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start positive/platform-first rather than in conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Starting with a positive platform is easier to build; starting immediately in conflict can prevent the scene from moving forward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keith urges starting positive because it's easier to break the routine when trouble arrives. If starting in negativity, find the affinity between characters to create contrast and a path forward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break routines—raise stakes and generate change
rubrics_metrics.description: Scenes must avoid drifting back to neutral; energy must build, stakes must be raised and routines must be broken so characters change and a story develops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques: introduce an arbitrary change in emotion, a tilt, force a character reversal, or add a cost to a choice. Example: one character gives up (refuses the routine) which then needs justification and creates interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use tilts to introduce mystery and propel the story
rubrics_metrics.description: A tilt (a bizarre or specific change) can create mystery that propels action forward and gives new material to work with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Sally says 'I'm your soul'—this tilt raises questions the audience wants answered and forces characters to justify choices; tilts should be followed through to affect characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find the affinity when stuck in negativity
rubrics_metrics.description: When characters are in conflict or negativity, discovering an affinity between them provides contrast and can break the routine without losing dramatic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Andy Eninger’s tip: finding affinity sometimes reduces energy but, with right timing, can be moving and effective in advancing the scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Play multiple attitudes within a scene for transitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Skilled improvisers can shift attitudes (e.g., sentimental to cat, demanding to vet) within one scene, and audiences enjoy transitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use attitude changes to create movement and variety; training games like 'Sexy Smelly Stupid' prepare improvisers for switching attitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and building tension matter—don’t squander the process of change
rubrics_metrics.description: Scenes often require a build-up of tension and a well-timed breaking point; misuse of timing wastes the opportunity for satisfying changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shoe shop example: build up to someone cracking (shopkeeper or customer) and time the break to create payoff (free pair, reveal, collapse).

rubrics_metrics.name: Directorial intervention: change someone when characters are too similar
rubrics_metrics.description: If two players create very similar characters, the coach/director should intervene and ask someone to change to create contrast and narrative movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early coach corrections prevent scenes from stalling; be confident in directing players away from trivializing or sticking to sameness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify reversals—weak choices must have cost or reason
rubrics_metrics.description: When a character makes a sudden reversal (e.g., gives up), the reversal must be justified—adding a cost or motive makes the choice strong and meaningful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relate to hero’s journey template: refusal then acceptance with cost. Use justification to make moral or significant choices feel earned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid cancelling offers and unexplained frame-breaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Sudden cancellation of repeatedly-established offers (e.g., a bully who suddenly becomes servile without reason) or frame-breaking devices (e.g., 'it was all a dream' or 'it was a TV show') risks abandoning character and story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although bold frame breaks can sometimes be rewarding, they often leave the audience confused unless properly justified; distinguish revealing character (good) from canceling offers (bad) and gagging (awful).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not gag excessively or rely on gratuitous frame-breaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Gagging (prioritising a quick joke over story/character) and gratuitous frame-breaking tend to undermine character revelation and story development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monty Python-style frame-breaking frequently escapes the need to develop story into the future; use sparingly and with justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep slip contents private to simulate unaided strong characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Keeping what’s written on slips private mimics performing without a crutch and introduces the same problems improvisers will face in real shows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Privacy forces players to rely on internalisation and partners’ offers rather than visible prompts; you can reveal slips in 'training wheels' phases then move to private slips.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character is malleable—all actions can be justified
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the cliché 'my character wouldn’t do that'—almost no action is beyond justification; changes reveal new sides of characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a character does something new, commit and find a believable justification; transformations are a core source of story and audience satisfaction.
